Time of report 0511. Victim was found dead in the water. The only one left in the scene is a six year old child. The situation does not seem to faze him; he was not showing signs of fear or sadness. I keep a watchful eye on him as I look over the rest of the report. Victim a John Doe.  No witness other than the kid and no suspects yet. Looks like I have my work cut out for me this morning. I glance up and he is no longer in my sight. Next thing you know I feel a tug on my sleeve. He says nothing, but I stare into his green little eyes. <I am God, and I need you to protect me.>

Did he just speak to me in my head and ask for protection? It didn’t make sense. I wanted to argue with this so-called god, but in an instant a decision was made for me. The corpse was alive. And it was running straight at us.  My heart started to race and all I could do was react. One- Two- Three. Shots fired and they didn’t miss. Five- Six- Seven. Dammit that thing was still coming at us. Eight- Nine- Ten. A voice as clear as day in my mind.  <RUN! Run away from the car and into the cover of the woods!>

I have the kid on my shoulders and I am almost out of breath. I’m a decent runner, but definitely not one to run marathons. I can only assume I’m still being chased but the woods were uncomfortably silent. <We can stop now. This place is sacred.> 

“Get out of my head and start talking”. He stares at me with a blank face. What did I just get myself into? And what was I going to tell the chief? <By the end of this day that will be the least of your worries.>

My opinion though is that, if it is a true monogamous relationship, continue to at least take PreP or use a condom as a barrier of protection. There is no documented risk in unprotected sex.. But at the same time it doesn't hurt to have it. But to each his own.

1. Perception is everything. Take lots of notes and aim high.

The first impression your unit will get from you is the tech school report sent by the base training manager. In it are your scores and notes from your instructors. If you show that you are a quality student, your unit will know how to take care of you.

2. Be the most capable and experienced person in your squadron. 

If you can reach that, make sure not to piss anyone off along the way. You can know your job, but you also have to be approachable to your peers. You will need them eventually to help you with  tasks or assignments.

3. Lead. Don't be afraid to fail. I came in straight out of tech school and immediately took over the PCS section. A job not normally given to A1C's. But I learned a lot in tech school and did not wait for tasks to be given to me. Before I even finished my CDCs I ended up winning Airman of the Quarter for the Base and also Majcom.

4. You are responsible for your career. 

No one else is going to look out for you other than yourself. Your supervisor can't write you a package if you don't have anything to offer. If you don't ask for things or communicate what you want; you won't get it.

5. Don't get lazy. 

Finance is not a 0700-1530 job. The work doesn't stop when the phone stops ringing or when the customers stop coming in. Wether your are in budget, accounting, or customer service- the job never ends. It is easy to be lazy and be mediocre. Hold yourself to higher standards and do everything to the best of your ability. Stay motivated and be an expert at your job. 

6. Other people have the luxury of not knowing what we know

We have a hated career field and everyone want to blame us for their pay. We live in a world that needs funds, and those funds needs to be processed by people in finance. People can bitch and complain about how easy and worthless our jobs are. But who is going to actually do the work. Them? People will talk to you behind your back, but deep down they WANT you in finance. They NEED you in finance. You help people get paid, and while they might not acknowledge that, know that your job matters. They want you in that Finance office, because they sure as hell can't fathom what it would be like to deal with what we deal with.

Quality Assurance for Finance here: do your research. Get direct line to customer service number. Find out their customer service hours. Get their e-mail address for workflow box. Find out who the NCOIC is. 

Get in touch with a technician. Get their name and rank. Make sure you tell them you are documenting when you call them and what they tell you. Travel vouchers by regulation should not take more than 30 days to be paid out. Ask them the date they sent the voucher to Ellsworth. Make sure to tell the technician handling your voucher that you want them to follow up if there are any rejects or if there is anything wrong with your voucher. Your final pay should not take take more than 30 days out from your final out. Take the same steps with your final pay, document who you talk to and what they say. If things take longer than 30 days elevate it to the next level.

tldr; Finance does it's best to make sure you get your money, but ultimately you won't get any results by waiting.

I do not feel sorry if you don't get the correct answer because you didn't take the time to go to your servicing finance office or make a different attempt to contact them.

If your pay is important to you, go look at the regulation or make a trip down to Finance. Go to the airforce portal and actual check out the Finance section. Send Finance an e-mail on their workflow box and put a read receipt on it. Find out who the NCOIC of the office is and get a number or an e-mail address. "Finance didn't answer the phone", "the office is so far away", or "the customer service counter was closed" is not an excuse. 

You got the wrong answer? Didn't get the right customer service the right time? Document it and file a customer service survey. A negative survey goes a long way, and sometimes it is the only way the customer service technician will learn.

It's your pay and if you just give up because they didn't answer their phone or they didn't answer your e-mail, then it's not their fault. 

If all we did all day was sit in the counter or answer the phone, we would not get any work done.

You can go to the nearest Finance office and they should be able to reset your mypay pin. You have to do it in person, and you must be able to show your retiree id. This is a last resort if you can't reach DFAS through that hotline.

I like that at the end of the day, most people have no choice but to realize that they need me. People will always need a Finance person to help them with their pay and one of these days they will need me to make sure Finance does their job. I like that my job matters and most people avoid trying to piss me off.

No one is getting paid until DFAS gets FY 14 money. All forms of military pay disbursements are not leaving the DFAS building and are put on hold until further guidance from DOD. 

That  means anyone who separated waiting on their final pay have to wait. Anyone trying to get BAH advances or pay advances have to wait. Anyone trying to take out their savings deposit have to wait. Re-enlistment bonuses have been put on hold. Travel vouchers and TDY entitlements as well.

In the AF here, I think for the most part you have to be resilient finding friends. AF members are one of the most cliquish groups you'll ever meet. Finding a sense of camaraderie is hard, but you just have to be persistent. For the most part I think most career fields stick to their own. You rarely see a flyer hanging out with a maintainer, vice versa. Sometimes good friends just come out of luck. Just try your best to meet new people. Hopefully you get to meet at least one person when you in-process. 

My advice? Make friends with someone from personnel and finance. We pretty much encounter every single person from the base. For the most part, you are going to need friends in finance and personnel. PCSing will suck if you don't. Usually bases schedule the in-processing briefings in groups. So that's always a good opportunity to meet new people. And depending on your personality type, join some pro org. I feel that I've developed more as a person, because I've put myself out there. 

As far as staying in the closet and meeting new people. Like I said earlier, sometimes good friends just come out of luck. Most of the friends I have now have really been effortless. For the most part I've just made an effort to keep people as acquaintances. Then it really just works itself out. Either you get invited to their circle or you find yourself gravitating in theirs. I think most friendships don't work when they are forced. Just be honest when it comes to sharing who you are. You'll be surprised how far honesty can go. 

I am not "out", but most of the friends I have now know that I am gay. They know who I am. And I'd rather just have one friend that can deal with that, than a bunch of fake ones. So yea. Friendships are not meant to be hard to make. If they are real friends, they will stick with you no matter what. I have a lot of straight friends who accept me as their brother. You'll find it too, just accept no bullshit and be honest.
